title: PQ urges other parties urged to sit in Quebec legislature — despite recent ruling ordering oath to King

blocks.text: Montreal·New

The battle over whether Quebec legislators will have to swear an oath to the King continues, with an appeal hearing scheduled for Friday. The premier wants his opponents to join him in sitting in the legislative session, regardless of the outcome of the court ruling.
Superior Court ruling suspended law that made oath optional; appeal to be heard Friday

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is encouraging his opponents to join him in taking their seats at the National Assembly next Tuesday, despite a Quebec Superior Court judge’s ruling ordering legislators to swear allegiance to the King before sitting at the National Assembly.
Justice Ian Demers warned on Monday that laws passed at the National Assembly could be rendered invalid if members do not take the oath.
The government is contesting the decision. The appeal will be heard at 2 p.m. on Friday in Montreal.
"We believe that, in any case, there is absolutely nothing preventing us from sitting," said Parti Québécois (PQ) parliamentary leader Catherine Gentilcore on Wednesday.

Even though the appeal has not yet been heard, the premier has sent a letter to the leaders of the three opposition parties, urging them to commit "to begin our parliamentary work on December 1, with our oaths as they currently stand."
During the swearing-in ceremonies of each party, the MNAs made their oaths to the Quebec people. It was Bill 4, passed unanimously in Quebec in Dec. 2022, that made the oath to the Crown optional.

Demers said in his Monday ruling, though, that the Quebec government had overstepped its constitutional boundaries with this law. He wrote that "the Constitution is not an à la carte menu" from which individuals can pick and choose what to follow.

Could the Parti Québécois actually abolish the monarchy in Quebec?

blocks.text: All the parties have said they want the legislative session to start next Tuesday as planned. However, they've expressed varying degrees of resistance to pledging allegiance to King Charles.
Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard has said he won't rule out taking the oath.
"It wouldn't be responsible to close any doors except the one that we will not be postponing the session," he said on Tuesday.
Quebec Conservative Party Leader Éric Duhaime has voiced support for protecting the parliamentary sovereignty of the National Assembly, while also showing a willingness to be flexible.
"It's not because you know you're saying those words before you're getting into the House that necessarily you become a federalist and a monarchist," Duhaime said.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the province's political parties have reached an agreement to change another National Assembly rule.

When the premier marks the opening of the legislative session, the new Speaker of the National Assembly will table the written speech of the lieutenant-governor, who's a representative of the monarchy.
The lieutenant-governor has traditionally delivered an opening address at the start of a new legislative session.
